title: Systems Programming
description: Computer organisation, registers and ports; memory segments and x86 assembly language programming with NASM; processes, threads and concurrency; Java multithreading and synchronization; network programming with Java sockets; and Unix processes and inter-process communication. Built from the CSC 334 course book (Units 1 to 15); Unix processes, signals and IPC, which the 2024/25 paper tests, are added from general knowledge.

topics.title: Computer Organisation, Registers and Ports
topics.summary: A computer is organised into processor, memory and I/O, and registers sit at the top of the memory hierarchy as the fastest storage. Ports are the connection points for peripherals, serial or parallel, from PS/2 and DE-9 to USB, HDMI and RJ-45.
subtopics: Characteristics and limitations of systems programming
Registers: AC, DR, AR, PC, MDR, index register, MBR
Fetch, decode and execute; memory hierarchy and locality of reference
User-visible and control and status registers; the PSW flags
Serial and parallel ports; PS/2, DB-25 and DE-9
Video, audio, USB and network ports

topics.title: Memory Segments and Assembly Language Basics
topics.summary: A program's memory holds code (text), initialised data, uninitialised data (.bss), stack and heap segments. An assembly program has data, bss and text sections; NASM assembles it, and Linux system calls are made through registers and int 80h.
subtopics: Code, data, .bss, stack and heap segments
Object files: relocatable, executable, shared
Advantages of assembly language; binary and hexadecimal
Sections, statements and comments in NASM
IA-32 registers and flags
Assembling, linking and Linux system calls

topics.title: Assembly Instructions, Procedures and Macros
topics.summary: Instructions reach operands by register, immediate or memory addressing, and storage is set aside with define, reserve, TIMES and EQU directives. Arithmetic, logical, compare and jump instructions, loops, procedures, the stack and macros build complete programs.
subtopics: Register, immediate and memory addressing; MOV
Define and reserve directives, TIMES, EQU, %assign, %define
INC, DEC, ADD, SUB, MUL/IMUL, DIV/IDIV
AND, OR, XOR, TEST, NOT
CMP, JMP, conditional jumps and LOOP
Procedures, the stack, recursion and macros

topics.title: Processes, Threads and Concurrency
topics.summary: The OS tracks each process in a process list and PCB through creation, execution and termination. Threads are lightweight processes; concurrent execution interleaves them on one processor, while parallel execution runs them at the same time on several.
subtopics: Process list, PCB and context switch
Process creation and states
Threads and their advantages over processes
Concurrent and parallel execution; granularity
User and kernel threads; multithreading models
Uses and benefits of multithreading

topics.title: Java Threads and Synchronization
topics.summary: Java threads move through new, runnable, waiting, timed waiting and terminated states and are scheduled by priority and time slicing. Executors run Runnable tasks in thread pools, and locks and conditions synchronize threads that share data, as in the producer/consumer relationship.
subtopics: Thread states and the thread scheduler
Priorities, time slicing and preemption
Runnable, Executor and ExecutorService
Locks, ReentrantLock and the fairness policy
Conditions: await, signal, signalAll; deadlock
Producer/consumer with and without synchronization

topics.title: Network Programming in Java
topics.summary: Java's java.net package supports stream-based (TCP, connection-oriented) and packet-based (UDP, connectionless) communication. A server opens a ServerSocket and accepts clients on Socket streams; datagram programs exchange DatagramPackets.
subtopics: Client-server relationship; java.net
Stream sockets and datagram sockets
Manipulating URLs and reading a file on a web server
Establishing a server: the five steps
Establishing a client: the four steps
Connectionless communication with datagrams

topics.title: Unix Processes, Signals and IPC
topics.summary: Unix creates processes with fork() and runs new programs with exec(), managing them from creation to termination. Signals notify processes asynchronously, and processes exchange data through pipes, message queues, shared memory and sockets.
subtopics: fork(), exec() and vfork()
The Unix process lifecycle; zombies and orphans
Signals and signal handling
IPC: pipes, FIFOs, message queues, semaphores, sockets
Shared memory
File handling and number conversion in C
